title: Half state at $ν_{tot}$ = -1/2 and its transition in Decoupled Twisted Double Bilayer Graphene
authors: Ning Ma, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Mitali Banerjee
abstract: The origin of the fractional state at $ν$ = 1/2 observed in double-layer quantum Hall systems has been under debate for decades. Because of the variation of bilayer charge distribution and interlayer tunneling strength, the half-filling state can be attributed to a two-component(2C) or a one-component(1C) origin, which corresponds to Halperin state and Pffafian state, respectively. Here we report the magnetotransport measurement in decoupled twisted double bilayer graphene(TDBG), which has been proved to be a promising platform for double quantum Hall system. Fractional quantum hall states in both odd and even denominator fillings are observed. We also found that the half-filling state occurs at zero displacement field at $ν_{tot}$ = -1/2, which is theoretically consistent with two-component Halperin-Laughlin (Ψ331) state. Moreover, we report the transition from two-component state at zero D field to one-component non-Abelian state by tunning displacement field. Our observation of the half filling state and its transition from 2C to 1C state provides the tunability of decoupled twisted double bilayer graphene and shed light on the understanding of the ground states at half-filling factor in the double quantum Hall system.
summary:
This work reports magnetotransport measurements on decoupled twisted double bilayer graphene to investigate fractional quantum Hall states. The key finding is the observation of a controllable transition at half-filling ($
u_{tot}=-1/2$) from a two-component Abelian state to a one-component non-Abelian state by tuning an external displacement field. This demonstrates that TDBG is a tunable platform for studying fundamental correlated electron physics.
main_problem:
The study aims to resolve the long-standing debate regarding the origin of the half-filling fractional quantum Hall state ($
u_{tot} = -1/2$) in double quantum Hall systems, specifically distinguishing between two-component (Halperin) and one-component (Pfaffian) origins.
main_result:
The authors observed that at zero displacement field ($D=0$), the $
u_{tot}=-1/2$ state is consistent with a two-component Halperin-Laughlin state, which undergoes a transition to a one-component non-Abelian state when a finite displacement field is applied.
method: Magnetotransport measurements (longitudinal resistance) were performed as a function of total carrier density and an out-of-plane magnetic field, supplemented by temperature dependence measurements to extract activation gaps.
model_or_system: The physical platform utilized is Decoupled Twisted Double Bilayer Graphene (TDBG), which serves as a tunable model for double quantum Hall systems due to its controllable interlayer coupling and orbital degrees of freedom.
key_observables:
Resistive minima in $
u_{tot}-D$ maps, thermal activation gaps ($\Delta$), and the transition between 2C and 1C state signatures.
important_parameters:
Total filling factor ($
u_{tot}$), displacement field ($D$), magnetic field strength ($B \approx 10 	ext{ T}$), and temperature range (350 mK to 1 K).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed transitions are governed by polarization induced by the displacement field, which breaks interlayer coherence between different correlated states.
figures_summary:
Figures show $
u_{tot}-D$ maps revealing integer and fractional Hall states; temperature dependence plots confirm distinct activation gaps for various fillings ($
u=-8/3, -7/3, -5/2$); and specific plots illustrate the transition of the half-filling state with applied $D$.
paper_structure:
The paper systematically presents magnetotransport measurements across varying filling factors and displacement fields. It first establishes the observation of various fractional states (Jain sequence) and then focuses on the $
u_{tot}=-1/2$ state, detailing its transition from a 2C to a 1C non-Abelian state as $D$ is tuned.
why_interesting: The ability to tune between different topological ground states (Abelian vs. non-Abelian) using an external electric field ($D$) in a solid-state system like graphene makes this highly relevant for realizing and controlling exotic quantum phases of matter.
